title: What is one twelfth times one eighteenth?
description: The video finds one twelfth times one eighteenth without drawing the unit square, by multiplying the rows and the columns. Keeko then raises a hand with the doubt that the bottoms can be added.
teaching_notes: One idea: the number of equal parts is the product of the two bottoms, and one part is shaded, so the product has one on top. Watch for students who add the bottoms.

source: Find 1/12 × 1/18 without drawing the unit square.
video_script.why: The child has counted rows times columns in drawn squares and now does the same count without drawing.
video_script.substitution: The unit square would have eighteen rows and twelve columns, so two hundred sixteen equal parts, and one part is shaded.
video_script.anchor: Find one twelfth times one eighteenth without drawing the square
video_script.wrong_move: adds the bottoms, twelve and eighteen, and gets one thirtieth, which is far bigger than one two hundred sixteenth
video_script.payoff_line: One twelfth times one eighteenth is one two hundred sixteenth
video_script.fraction_reading: one twelfth, one eighteenth, one two hundred sixteenth, one thirtieth
maths_rules: unit square for 1/12 × 1/18: 18 rows and 12 columns
the slip: 12 + 18 = 30, and 1/30 is far bigger than 1/216
video_script.design: One idea: the bottoms multiply to give the number of equal parts, and one part is shaded. The faint unit square is the anchor and stays all video; the working band builds in the idea part.

narration: <bookmark mark='pic'/>Step one, picture the unit square for this product.
<bookmark mark='rc'/>It would have eighteen rows and twelve columns.
<bookmark mark='mult'/>Step two, count all the equal parts by multiplying the rows and the columns.
Eighteen times twelve is two hundred sixteen.

beats.on_screen: Step 3: 1 part is shaded, so the top is 1 and the bottom is 216

marks.bottom: the top 1 and the bottom 216 are written as a fraction bar

narration: <bookmark mark='one'/>Step three, only one part is shaded, so the top of the answer is one.
<bookmark mark='bottom'/>The bottom is the number of equal parts, which is two hundred sixteen.

marks.pay: the answer stays on the board

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>In general, two such fractions give one on top and the two bottoms multiplied below.
<bookmark mark='pay'/>One twelfth times one eighteenth is one two hundred sixteenth.

beats.on_screen: Keeko with a raised hand beside the answer
narration: <bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: 1/12 × 1/18 = 1/30 is written and crossed out; the square with 18 rows of 12 parts is shown again

marks.fix: the square with 18 rows of 12 parts glows and the line is crossed out

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks the answer is one thirtieth.
Keeko added the bottoms, twelve and eighteen.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>But the square has eighteen rows, and each row has twelve parts.
That is far more than thirty parts.
<bookmark mark='rule'/>Multiply the bottoms to count the parts, and do not add them.
